entry.reasons: The definition of tension is factual and directly matches the CED Essential Knowledge statement 2.3.A.3. The topic codes are correct, as tension is introduced in Topic 2.3 and applied to circular motion (conical pendulum) in Topic 2.9 (EK 2.9.A.2.iii).

The body matches 2.3.A.3: “Tension is the macroscopic net result of forces that segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other in response to an external force.” Topic 2.3 first requires the definition, and 2.9.A.2.iii uses tension in a conical pendulum. No caution is needed because the body uses the CED wording.

a_factual: The body matches 2.3.A.3 ('Tension is the macroscopic net result of forces that segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other in response to an external force'). The only difference is the added article 'the' before 'forces', which does not change the content. b_topic_codes: Topic 2.3 is where tension is first required (2.3.A.3, with the ideal-string and ideal-pulley statements). Topic 2.9 also uses tension: 2.9.A.2.iii states 'A component of tension contributes to the net force producing centripetal acceleration experienced by a conical pendulum.' c_ced_required: 2.3.A.3 requires students to describe tension in a string, cable, chain, or similar system, so the definition is CED-required. d_caution: The wording is nearly verbatim to the CED, so the point-earning wording is effectively the same and no caution is needed. The null caution is correct.

The definition of an ideal string and its tension properties are directly supported by Essential Knowledge statements 2.3.A.3.i and 2.3.A.3.ii. The caution accurately reflects the boundary statement regarding qualitative descriptions of strings with nonnegligible mass (e.g., hanging chains).

Topic 2.3.A.3.i states, “An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch when under tension,” and 2.3.A.3.ii states that its tension is the same at all points. The caution matches 2.3.A.3.iii and the boundary statement limiting descriptions of tension in a string with mass to qualitative ones. Topic 2.3 is the correct owner and listed topic.

a_factual: The body matches 2.3.A.3.i ('An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch when under tension') and 2.3.A.3.ii ('The tension in an ideal string is the same at all points within the string'). The body joins these with 'so', a causal link the CED does not state as such. The link is physically sound, so it is noted but does not make the content incorrect. b_topic_codes: Tension is introduced under Topic 2.3 (Newton's Third Law, essential knowledge 2.3.A.3), so owner_topic_code 2.3 is correct and topic_codes ['2.3'] is correct. c_ced_required: 2.3.A.3.i-ii are required essential knowledge under LO 2.3.A, so the entry is CED-required. d_caution: The CED boundary statement says AP Physics 1 only expects a qualitative description of tension in strings with mass, e.g., 'the tension in a hanging chain is greater toward the top of the chain.' The caution reproduces this correctly. The entry's wording ('does not stretch under tension') also differs slightly from the CED's 'when under tension', and the caution covers the point that matters. accept: all booleans true.

The definition of an ideal pulley matches the exact wording of Essential Knowledge 2.3.A.3.iv in the CED: 'An ideal pulley is a pulley that has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction.'

The body matches Essential Knowledge 2.3.A.3.iv: “An ideal pulley is a pulley that has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction.” Topic 2.3 is the cited location, and the wording needs no caution.

a_factual: The body matches CED 2.3.A.3.iv, which states that an ideal pulley has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction. The body drops the CED's leading 'is a pulley that', but the content and list of conditions are unchanged. b_topic_codes: 2.3.A.3.iv appears under Topic 2.3 (Newton's Third Law), so owner_topic_code '2.3' is correct and is the only topic that uses it. c_ced_required: 2.3.A.3.iv is an essential-knowledge statement, and the ideal-pulley assumptions are needed to apply tension in pulley problems under LO 2.3.A. d_caution: The entry's wording is a close paraphrase that keeps the same meaning as the CED sentence. The entry accurately reflects the essential knowledge statements 2.5.A.2 ('the acceleration of a system’s center of mass... is in the same direction as that net force') and 2.5.A.3 ('The velocity of a system’s center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system') from the CED.

Topic 2.5 first requires the entry’s acceleration-direction claim: 2.5.A.2 says the center-of-mass acceleration is “in the same direction as that net force.” The velocity-change claim matches 2.5.A.3: velocity “will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system.” The wording needs no caution.

a_factual: Matches 2.5.A.2 ('the acceleration of a system's center of mass ... is in the same direction as that net force') and 2.5.A.3 ('The velocity of a system's center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system'). No formula or list is involved. b_topic_codes: 2.5 is the topic where these statements appear in Unit 2, and it is the only topic listed. c_ced_required: 2.5.A.2 and 2.5.A.3 are essential knowledge statements under LO 2.5.A, which requires students to apply the direction and velocity-change conditions. d_caution: fails. The CED specifies the velocity of a system's center of mass, but the body says 'its velocity changes', which drops the center-of-mass qualifier. That qualifier matters because internal forces can change the motion of parts of a system without changing the center-of-mass velocity (2.3.A.2: 'Interactions between objects within a system (internal forces) do not influence the motion of a system's center of mass'). The wording differs from the point-earning wording, so a caution is required and none is present. The first clause ('center-of-mass acceleration') is correct, so the fix is to restore 'center of mass' in the second clause or add a caution explaining that only the center-of-mass velocity is governed by net external force.

The first clause is correct. CED 2.5.A.2: the acceleration of a system's center of mass 'is in the same direction as that net force.' The second clause misstates the CED. CED 2.5.A.3 says 'The velocity of a system's center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system.' The entry drops 'of center of mass' and says 'its velocity changes only if...', which applied to a whole system is wrong. CED 2.3.A.2 says internal forces do not influence the motion of a system's center of mass, and 2.1.A.4 says individual parts may behave differently from the system as a whole, so 'its velocity' can change without an external net force. The entry is therefore not factually faithful, and the wording that earns the point ('velocity of a system's center of mass') is not used. A caution would be needed to point this out, but caution is null. b_topic_codes is fine: 2.5 is where Unit 2 first requires this, and Topic 2.5 uses it. c_ced_required is satisfied by 2.5.A.2 and 2.5.A.3. The entry is rejected because the second clause must say 'velocity of the system's center of mass' and/or carry a caution.

The entry accurately reflects the requirements for free-body diagrams as detailed in Topic 2.2 (EK 2.2.B.1 through 2.2.B.4) and the associated boundary statement. It correctly highlights the rules regarding drawing forces from the dot, avoiding components, drawing same-direction forces side-by-side, and aligning coordinate axes with acceleration.

The diagram content matches Topic 2.2: 2.2.B.2 says an FBD shows each force exerted by the environment, and the boundary statement requires separate straight arrows originating on the dot, with same-direction forces side by side rather than overlapping. The caution is not fully supported by the supplied CED pages. They use Fg and state “Weight = Fg = mg,” but do not establish that F_G or W are accepted labels or that G or g alone are not accepted.

Topic 2.2 requires free-body diagrams. The CED says a diagram shows “each of the forces exerted on the object by the environment” (2.2.B.2), with vectors originating from the representation of the center of mass (2.2.B.3). Its boundary statement requires individual straight arrows from the dot, same-direction arrows side by side rather than overlapping, and forces rather than force components. Section 2.2.B.4 supports the coordinate-axis guidance. The caution correctly distinguishes gravity from a separate ‘net centripetal force’ arrow; the CED explicitly gives Fg = mg for weight (2.6.A.3), though it does not prescribe an exhaustive list of acceptable force labels.

a_factual: The body matches CED 2.2.B.2 ('The free-body diagram of an object or system shows each of the forces exerted on the object by the environment') and 2.2.B.3 (forces 'represented as vectors originating from the representation of the center of mass, such as a dot'). The items match the boundary statement: individual straight arrows originating on the dot, same-direction forces drawn side by side and not overlapping, whole forces rather than components. The axis item matches 2.2.B.4 ('one axis parallel to the direction of acceleration... for example... parallel to the surface of the incline'). b_topic_codes: 2.2 is where Unit 2 first introduces the FBD (2.2.B.1), and topic 2.2 is the only code listed. c_ced_required: LO 2.2.B ('Describe the forces exerted on an object or system using a free-body diagram') and 2.2.B.1 require students to use FBDs. d_caution: fails. The caution asserts that labels must be F_g, F_G, W or mg and that 'G' or 'g' alone is 'not accepted'. No CED page states a labelling or scoring rule of this kind. The CED only gives weight = F_g = mg (2.6.A.3) and the gravitational-force symbol in 2.6.A.1. The 'net centripetal force' arrow prohibition is a reasonable inference from 2.2.B.2 but is also not stated on the CED pages. The unsupported scoring claim makes the caution incorrect as written. Remove or re-source the label-acceptance claim and the caution can pass.

a_factual: The body matches CED 2.2.B.2 ('The free-body diagram of an object or system shows each of the forces exerted on the object by the environment') and 2.2.B.3 (forces are vectors originating from a dot at the center of mass). The items match the Boundary Statement under 2.2.B: individual forces are 'individual straight arrows, originating on the dot and pointing in the direction of the force'; same-direction forces are 'drawn side by side, not overlapping'; and 'depict the forces exerted on objects, not the force components.' The coordinate-axis item matches 2.2.B.4. b_topic_codes: Topic 2.2 is the first unit topic that introduces and requires the FBD (2.2.B.1), and 2.2 is the only code listed. c_ced_required: 2.2.B.1 requires students to describe forces on an object using an FBD, so this is required. d_caution: fails. The caution's first rule ('Label gravity F_g, F_G, W or mg; \'G\' or \'g\' alone is not accepted') is a labelling/scoring rule that does not appear on any of the supplied CED pages. The CED only supplies the symbols F_g, mg, and Weight (2.6.A.1, 2.6.A.3), so the claim that a bare 'g' or 'G' is rejected is unsupported by the source. The second rule (no separate 'net centripetal force' arrow) is a reasonable inference from 2.2.B.2 but is not stated in the CED. A caution must be correct to the CED, and this one asserts a rule the CED does not state. Remove the unsupported label rule or source it to an official scoring guideline, then resubmit.

The formula accurately represents Newton's second law of motion as described in Essential Knowledge 2.5.A.2, which states that the acceleration of a system's center of mass is proportional to the net force exerted on the system. The topic codes are correct as Newton's second law is fundamental to analyzing gravitational forces (Topic 2.6) and circular motion (Topic 2.9).

Topic 2.5.A.2 states that the acceleration of a system’s center of mass is proportional to, and in the direction of, the net force exerted on the system; the formula expresses Newton’s second law. Topic 2.6 applies force and acceleration to gravity, including 2.6.A.2.ii, and Topic 2.9 applies them to circular motion, including 2.9.A.2. No caution is needed.

a_factual: The formula a = ΣF/m_sys = F_net/m_sys is the standard Newton's second law and matches the CED's statement that the acceleration has magnitude proportional to the net force and is in the same direction (2.5.A.2). The CED's relevant equation is an image that does not survive text extraction, so the symbols were checked against the verbal statement only. b_topic_codes: 2.5 is the first unit-2 topic that introduces Newton's second law (2.5.A.2), so it is the correct owner. 2.6 (apparent weight in accelerating systems, 2.6.C.2) and 2.9 (centripetal net force, 2.9.A.1.i with F = mv²/r) both apply it. c_ced_required: 2.5.A.2 requires students to apply this relation. d_caution: The CED's point-earning wording is 'the acceleration of a system's center of mass'. The body uses a_sys, which hides the center-of-mass qualifier, and caution is null. A caution stating that a is the acceleration of the system's center of mass (and that the net force is the vector sum of external forces) is needed, so this check fails. Fix: add the center-of-mass caution (ideally using a_cm notation to match the CED) and re-review.

a_factual: The symbols and form match the CED's 2.5.A.2 statement that the acceleration of a system's center of mass is proportional to the magnitude of the net force on the system and in the same direction. The CED's 'Relevant equation' image is not in the extracted text, so the exact typeset form cannot be confirmed here; the standard form a = ΣF/m_sys is consistent with the text. b_topic_codes: 2.5 is the first unit topic that introduces Newton's second law (2.4 covers only the zero-net-force case), so owner 2.5 is correct. 2.6 (2.6.C.2, apparent weight of an accelerating system) and 2.9 (2.9.A.2, net force producing centripetal acceleration) use the law, though not with this exact equation stated. c_ced_required: 2.5.A.2 gives this as a 'Relevant equation' that students must apply, so the requirement is met. d_caution: The CED says the acceleration is of 'a system's center of mass' and the net force is 'exerted on the system' (2.5.A.2, and 2.5.A.3 specifies a 'nonzero net external force'). The entry uses a_sys and F_net without stating that a is the center-of-mass acceleration or that ΣF means the net external force. The point-earning wording therefore differs from the entry, and no caution is present. The second equality, F_net/m_sys, is also just a restatement of the first. A caution is required, so the entry is rejected for d_caution.

Topic 2.6.A.3 gives the derived equation “Weight = Fg = mg,” so the formula is correct and required in its assigned topic. The caution makes unsupported exam-acceptance claims: the provided CED specifies how to draw force arrows on free-body diagrams (Topic 2.2 boundary statement), but does not say that F_G or W is accepted as a label, or that G or g alone is not accepted.

Topic 2.6.A.3 explicitly gives the derived equation “Weight = Fg = mg,” so the formula is correct, required, and correctly assigned to 2.6. The entry accurately reflects the essential knowledge statements 2.7.A.1.i ('The kinetic friction force is exerted in a direction opposite to the motion of each surface relative to the other surface') and 2.7.A.1.ii ('The force of friction between two surfaces does not depend on the size of the surface area of contact') from the AP Physics 1 CED.

Topic 2.7.A.1.i states that kinetic friction is exerted opposite to the motion of each surface relative to the other. Topic 2.7.A.1.ii states that friction does not depend on the size of the surface area of contact. Both claims are required in Topic 2.7, and the entry needs no caution.

a_factual: The body matches 2.7.A.1.i, 'The kinetic friction force is exerted in a direction opposite to the motion of each surface relative to the other surface,' and 2.7.A.1.ii, 'The force of friction between two surfaces does not depend on the size of the surface area of contact.' The body states the direction relative to the other surface, as the CED does, so the convention is not misstated. b_topic_codes: Kinetic friction is introduced in Topic 2.7 (LO 2.7.A), so owner_topic_code '2.7' is where it is first required, and topic_codes ['2.7'] is the only topic that uses it. c_ced_required: LO 2.7.A ('Describe kinetic friction between two surfaces') and its essential knowledge 2.7.A.1.i/ii require students to apply both the direction convention and the independence from contact area. d_caution: The body is a paraphrase, but it carries the same direction convention and the same area-independence statement as the CED, so the point-earning content is present. No caution is needed. The entry is not a restatement with a different meaning.
The entry accurately defines apparent weight and weightlessness in strict accordance with Topic 2.6 (specifically EK 2.6.C.1, 2.6.C.2, and 2.6.C.3).

Topic 2.6.C.1 defines apparent weight as the magnitude of the normal force. 2.6.C.2 states that if a system is accelerating, its apparent weight is not equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force. The caution matches 2.6.C.3: a system appears weightless when no forces act on it or gravity is the only force.

a_factual: The body matches CED 2.6.C.1, 'The magnitude of the apparent weight of a system is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system.' It also matches the accelerating condition in 2.6.C.2, 'If the system is accelerating, the apparent weight of the system is not equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on the system.' b_topic_codes: Apparent weight is introduced under Topic 2.6 (learning objective 2.6.C). Topic 2.5 mentions only normal force and does not treat apparent weight, so 2.6 is the first unit location and the only topic code is correct. c_ced_required: Learning objective 2.6.C ('Describe the conditions under which the magnitude of a system's apparent weight is different from the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on that system') requires students to apply this idea. d_caution: The body is a faithful paraphrase of 2.6.C.1, so no caution is strictly required. The caution is present and accurate: it matches 2.6.C.3, 'A system appears weightless when there are no forces exerted on the system or when the force of gravity is the only force exerted on the system.' It targets the common misconception that weightlessness means gravity is absent.
The formula correctly represents the relationship between period, speed, radius, and frequency for uniform circular motion as described in Essential Knowledge statements 2.9.A.5.ii and 2.9.A.5.iii.

Topic 2.9.A.5.ii gives T = 1/f, and 2.9.A.5.iii states, “For an object traveling at a constant speed in a circular path, the period is given by the derived equation.” The period is the circumference 2πr divided by constant speed v. Topic 2.9 is the correct owner and only listed topic. The caution correctly states the constant-speed condition for T = 2πr/v.

a_factual: T = 2πr/v = 1/f is the correct period relation for uniform circular motion. T = 1/f is stated verbatim in 2.9.A.5.ii ('Relevant equation: T = 1/f'). The derived form T = 2πr/v is the equation that 2.9.A.5.iii introduces as 'the derived equation'; its typeset form is an image not present in the extracted text, but it is the standard result and matches the CED's description (constant speed, circular path). b_topic_codes: 2.9 is the only topic that uses this, and 2.9.A.5 (period and frequency) is where it first appears in this unit. c_ced_required: 2.9.A.5.iii requires students to apply the period relation for an object at constant speed in a circular path. d_caution: 'Valid only for constant speed (uniform circular motion)' matches the CED's qualifier 'For an object traveling at a constant speed in a circular path', so the caution is present and correct.

The owner_topic_code is set to 2.7, but the normal force is first explicitly introduced and required in Topic 2.6 (specifically in EK 2.6.C.1: 'The magnitude of the apparent weight of a system is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system.'). Therefore, the owner_topic_code should be 2.6.

The definition of normal force is factually accurate and directly matches Essential Knowledge 2.7.A.2.ii. The topic codes are correct as the term is introduced in Topic 2.7 and applied to circular motion in Topic 2.9 (EK 2.9.A.2.ii). The caution is highly relevant to AP Physics 1 scenarios such as vertical loops.

The body matches 2.7.A.2.ii: normal force is perpendicular to the contact surface and 'directed away from the surface.' Topic 2.7 first defines it, and 2.9.A.2.ii uses it in circular motion. The caution’s loop example is too categorical: the normal force points downward at the top only for an object contacting the inside of the loop. Moreover, 2.9.A.2.i says that at the minimum speed there, 'the gravitational force is the only force that causes the centripetal acceleration,' so the normal force is zero.

The body matches 2.7.A.2.ii: normal force is the perpendicular component of the surface’s force, directed away from the surface. But 2.6.C.1 already requires the concept: apparent weight is 'the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system,' so 2.7 is not the first topic that requires it. Topic 2.9 also uses normal force in 2.9.A.2.ii. The caution’s loop example needs a qualification: at the top of an inside loop the normal force can point downward, but 'away from the surface' does not make that true for every vertical-loop arrangement.
